stories.headline: A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846
stories.dek: Two county histories record a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus” at Cassopolis, Michigan, in the spring of 1846: four charter members named, a ball of two hundred badges, and a date earlier than any lodge of the order we have been able to find in print. Here is the whole record, what it does and does not prove, and the questions still open.
pic: /img/news/e-clampus-vitus-in-cassopolis-1846
Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875, page 253: the first secret society of which there is any record
Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (1875), p. 253.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. In 1875 the first history of Cass County, Michigan, printed a short account of “the first Secret Society, of which there is any record” in the county: a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus,” instituted at Cassopolis in the spring of 1846. Seven years later a second county history printed it again. Neither book was written for the order now known as E Clampus Vitus, and so far as we can find, no historian of that order has ever cited either one.

At a glance

What
A lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus”
Where
Cassopolis, the county seat of Cass County, Michigan
When
Instituted in the spring of 1846; collapsed in 1847; revived in 1860 as “The Brothers of Charity”
Charter members
Dr. E. J. Bonine, Laban Harter, J. P. Osborn and Dr. L. Osborn
The ball
Winter of 1846–47, at the Union Hotel: “over two hundred badges”
First printed
Rogers, History of Cass County (1875), pp. 253–254, from an account by James M. Shepard
Printed again
Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 174
Why it matters
Earlier than every lodge of the order for which we have found a documented date, east or west

On this page

  3. The four founders

## The record

This is the passage as Alfred Mathews printed it in 1882, page 174, under the heading “The Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus.” A footnote credits it to “James M. Shepard, in Roger’s ‘History of Cass County.’” It is reproduced in full; the page photographs are below.

“The first secret society of which there is any record was a lodge of the Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus, which was instituted in the spring of 1846 with Dr. E. J. Bonine, Laban Harter, J. P. Osborn and Dr. L. Osborn as charter members.

“The order was in broadest burlesque of legitimate secret organizations, and was afterward merged in the ‘Sons of Malta,’ which died from exposure (by Frank Leslie) in the next decade.

“The candidates for admission were bound fast, blindfolded and dragged into the hall by halters. They were placed in the most ludicrous positions and required to pledge themselves to performances and courses of conduct which by a cunningly devised double entendre in the wording of the pledges were either impossible or eminently ridiculous.

“A peculiarity of human nature which renders the victim of a ‘sell’ restless and unhappy until he has inveigled others into the same meshes, insured the rapid growth and financial prosperity of this monstrous hoax. Numerous Neophites were found to assuage the grief and soothe the wounded pride of the earlier victims.

“A grand ball was given by the lodge in the winter of 1846–47, at the Union Hotel, at which over two hundred badges of the ‘Ancient and Honorable Order’ were displayed, and that, too, by men who stood the highest in popular esteem and respectability.

“The (dis)order collapsed in 1847, partly from lack of raw material and partly from a growing satiety amounting to disgust on the part of the better portion of the members, but it was successfully resurrected in 1860 under the alias of the ‘Brothers of Charity.’

“The second edition, although enlarged and improved, was of ‘few days and full of trouble’ to all except the charter members.”

The original, in Howard S. Rogers’s History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis, 1875), pages 253 and 254, differs in small ways that matter. Rogers prints the order’s name as “the ‘Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus,’” the respectable men as those who “stood among the highest,” and the last line as “to all except the charter (?) members.” The question mark is in the 1875 text; Mathews dropped it. The phrase “of few days, and full of trouble” is from the Book of Job (14:1), an old funeral text.
## Who wrote it

Mathews names the author: James M. Shepard. He did not see the lodge. Shepard was a small child in 1846 and came to Cassopolis only on 3 September 1868, as the village dentist; he later owned the county’s newspaper, the Cassopolis Vigilant (sole proprietor from 1878), and was elected to the Michigan Senate in 1878 (Glover, 1906, pp. 556–558). When he wrote, in about 1875, all three of the founders we can trace were still living in or near the county. The account is a written record of local memory, set down about thirty years after the events, and it should be read as that, not as a minute book.
## The four founders

DocumentedDr. Evan J. Bonine. Born at Richmond, Wayne County, Indiana, on 10 September 1821, of Quaker family; read medicine at Centreville, Indiana, and graduated from the Ohio Medical College at Cincinnati in 1843; married Eveline Beall in 1844 and practised at Cassopolis. He was twenty-four in the spring of 1846. In 1849 he went overland to California with his brother-in-law Laban Harter, and returned in 1851 to settle at Vandalia. He was surgeon of the 2nd Michigan Infantry in the Civil War, sat in the Michigan House for Cass County (1853) and Berrien County (1865–68, 1873) and in the Senate (1869–70), and was mayor and postmaster of Niles, where he died in December 1892. (Michigan Legislative Biography; Portrait and Biographical Record of Berrien and Cass Counties, 1893, quoting the Niles Daily Star.)

DocumentedLaban Harter. Of the four he is the least known. In the county histories of Cass and of Berrien he appears only on this charter. Two later records place him: an “L. Harter, Treasurer,” of the Niles Horse-Thief Association, organized in May 1853 (Ellis and Johnson, History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, 1880), and “the old Loban Harter residence” at Niles, where Bonine’s son Dr. Fred N. Bonine was born on 21 October 1863 (Niles Daily Star, obituary of Dr. Fred N. Bonine, 23 August 1941). Bonine’s 1892 obituary calls him Bonine’s brother-in-law. OpenThrough whom they were brothers-in-law, and Harter’s own dates, are not yet known.

DocumentedJ. P. Osborn: Jordan P. Osborn. Born 6 August 1823, a son of the Quaker minister Charles Osborn; named by Mathews as “Jordan P., who is a resident of Cassopolis,” and later a village trustee and, in 1876, President of the Village of Cassopolis. He was twenty-two in the spring of 1846. His elder brother Parker B. Osborn, born 1821, kept a harness shop at Cassopolis but removed to Wilmington, Ohio; the charter’s initials, J. P., point to Jordan.

DocumentedDr. L. Osborn: Dr. Leander Osborn, of Vandalia. Born 27 December 1825, a son of Josiah Osborn and grandson of Charles Osborn (Mathews, 1882). He began reading medicine with Dr. Bonine in 1847 and was afterward his partner for two years. He was twenty in the spring of 1846 and not yet a doctor: the title in the 1875 account is the one he held when it was written.

ReadingSo the lodge’s four were young men of one small circle: a young doctor, his brother-in-law, and two Osborns, one of them his future student. Two of the four, Bonine and Harter, would be in California within three years.
## The room

DocumentedThe Union Hotel was the frame tavern built by Eber Root, one of the first two men licensed to keep a tavern in Cassopolis, on 24 January 1832 (Rogers, 1875). It stood on the west side of Broadway at the public square (Glover, 1906). The 1860 wall map of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien counties prints one word on that block: HOTEL. Six years after the ball, on 12 June 1852, the county’s Masons held their first meeting “in the Union Hotel” (Mathews, 1882, p. 174): the kind of order the burlesque was made to mock, organizing under the same roof. The corner is still there; the hotel is not, and there is no marker. What became of the building is the subject of Case 2.
## What became of the lodge

DocumentedBy the account’s own words, the lodge collapsed in 1847 and was “resurrected in 1860 under the alias of the ‘Brothers of Charity,’” and the order “was afterward merged in the ‘Sons of Malta,’ which died from exposure (by Frank Leslie) in the next decade.”

ReadingThat merger needs care. No lodge of the Sons of Malta is dated before 1854 (a New Orleans lodge, November 1854), so the lodge of 1846, gone by 1847, cannot have merged into it. The revival of 1860 could have: the Sons of Malta were then at their height, and the exposure of their ritual in Frank Leslie’s Illustrated Newspaper early in 1860 is generally reckoned to have finished them. The account’s “in the next decade” is loose, but nothing in it is impossible.
## Where it fits in the order’s history

E Clampus Vitus is known today as the historical society of the old West, the “Clampers” whose plaques mark forgotten places across California and beyond. Its own history runs like this, and every date below is the order’s or its historians’, not ours.

DocumentedThe founding legend. The order traces itself to Ephraim Bee, innkeeper and blacksmith of West Union, in what is now West Virginia. The marker at West Union, put up in 2003, says that by legend Bee received his commission “around 1845.” No document from those years has been produced to date it. Jennifer Wilt of the Doddridge County Heritage Guild, working from the county’s court books and the period press, writes that “shortly after 1850” Bee proclaimed himself Grand Hototote, and that she has found newspaper references to the order “as early as 1853.” An 1896 account in the Parkersburg State Journal has its writer meeting Bee in the fall of 1847, and finding, when they met again “some years afterward,” that Bee “had concocted the celebrated secret order” in the meantime.

DocumentedThe eastern lodges. The order’s historian Hugh Shumate, as published by the Julia C. Bulette Chapter, writes: “There is documentation of lodges in Bedford Pennsylvania, (1847); Metropolis, Illinois (1849)” and Bowling Green, Missouri (1849); a lodge at Dahlonega, Georgia, is evidenced from a California newspaper of 7 March 1853.

DocumentedCalifornia. The order’s own 1966 history, Then and Now, says it “is generally accepted” that Joe Zumwalt brought the ritual to Hangtown (Placerville) in 1849, where a lodge “didn’t last,” and that he “did establish the first lodge of ECV by 1851” at Mokelumne Hill. Shumate dates the Hangtown attempt to 1850. The same book tells how Steamboat Jake, a merchant from Yreka, was brought “bound and blindfolded” before the “Hall of Comparative Ovations” in 1852.

DocumentedThe gap the order’s own history leaves. Then and Now says that travelling salesmen were taken into the order, “with or without authority from Bee,” and that by 1849 “the East and Middle West were dotted with Clamper Lodges.” It names none. Its closing postscript hopes that “some day someone will attempt to research and compile a complete list of the number and location of the lodges formed during this earlier period.”

ReadingRogers names one. A county seat in the Middle West, with a town, a season, a building, four names and a count of badges: Cassopolis, spring 1846. On the evidence we have been able to find, that is the earliest firmly dated lodge of the order in the surviving record, earlier than the order’s own documented dates in both the state of its founding and the state of its fame. We set it out as the first line of the list the order asked for in 1966.
## The spelling

Both Michigan histories spell the name “Eclampsus,” with an S. The order’s historian writes that Carl Wheat chose the present spelling, “Clampus,” in 1931, when the order was revived in San Francisco. The 2003 marker in Ephraim Bee’s own town still reads “E Clampsus Vitus.” The Michigan books are not misspelling the name; they spell it as it was spelled before 1931.
## A timeline

• 24 Jan 1832 Eber Root licensed to keep a tavern at Cassopolis; he builds the frame house that becomes the Union Hotel.
  • c. 1845 The order’s legend: Ephraim Bee’s commission. (Undated in any surviving record.)
  • Spring 1846 The Cassopolis lodge is instituted: Bonine, Harter, J. P. Osborn and L. Osborn.
  • Winter 1846–47 The grand ball at the Union Hotel: “over two hundred badges.”
  • 1847 The lodge collapses. Bedford, Pennsylvania: the earliest dated eastern lodge. Leander Osborn begins reading medicine with Bonine.
  • 1847 (fall) The 1896 Parkersburg account’s first meeting with Bee.
  • 1849 Bonine and Harter go overland to California. Metropolis and Bowling Green lodges. Hangtown attempt (1966 history).
  • 1850 Hangtown attempt (Shumate). “Shortly after 1850”: Bee proclaims himself Grand Hototote (Wilt).
  • 1851 Mokelumne Hill: the first lasting lodge in California. Bonine returns to Michigan.
  • 12 Jun 1852 The Masons’ first meeting at Cassopolis, in the Union Hotel.
  • 1853 Earliest newspaper references to the order (Wilt).
  • 1854 Earliest dated lodge of the Sons of Malta.
  • 1860 The Cassopolis lodge revived as “The Brothers of Charity.” Frank Leslie exposes the Sons of Malta.
  • 1868 James M. Shepard comes to Cassopolis.
  • 1875 Rogers prints Shepard’s account.
  • 1882 Mathews prints it again, naming Shepard.
  • 1931 The order revived in San Francisco; Carl Wheat fixes the spelling “Clampus.”
  • 1966 Then and Now asks for a list of the early lodges.
## What we are not saying

• Not that the order was founded at Cassopolis. The account says a lodge of the order was “instituted” there. Rogers uses the same word on the same page for the Odd Fellows lodge instituted at Cassopolis in February 1847 under a dispensation from a Grand Master: a local lodge of an order that already existed.
  • Not that the evidence is like for like. The Cassopolis account is local memory written down about thirty years later by a man who was not there. Wilt’s dates come from contemporary court books and newspapers. Ours is a claim about the surviving record, not about what may have happened unrecorded.
  • Not that the question is closed. Two histories of the order have not yet been read for this: Lois Rather, Men Will Be Boys: The Story of E Clampus Vitus (Oakland, 1980), and Seth Slopes, E Clampus Vitus: Now and Then (1979). Either could hold an earlier eastern lodge. Until they are read, the claim is provisional.
  • Not that Bonine or Harter carried the order west. The dates line up; no document connects them to any California lodge.
If anyone can show a lodge of the order dated earlier than the spring of 1846, with a place and names, we will say so on this page, with thanks and with their name.
## Open questions
These are the questions we cannot yet answer. Each one says where the answer is most likely to be. If you can help with any of them, please write to us.

1. Is there an earlier lodge? Rather (1980) and Slopes (1979), by interlibrary loan; and the order’s papers in the Holt-Atherton Special Collections, University of the Pacific, Stockton.
  2. Who told Shepard? He came in 1868 and wrote in about 1875, when Bonine and both Osborns were still living. His own question mark after “charter” suggests he was not sure the lodge ever had one.
  3. Did anyone write it down in 1846? Cassopolis had two papers that year, The Literary News, a small sheet of gossip and humour, and the Cass County Advocate. Any surviving issue could carry a notice of the ball.
  4. Who was Laban Harter? His dates, his trade, and how he was Bonine’s brother-in-law. The Cass County marriage records begin in 1837; the 1850 census of Berrien County; Silverbrook Cemetery at Niles.
  5. Did Bonine or Harter meet the order in California? Bonine’s typescript “Journey to California” is listed at the Fort St. Joseph Museum, Niles, with a copy in the Merrill J. Mattes Library of the Oregon-California Trails Association. Has anyone seen their names in any early Clamper record?
  6. Does any badge survive? Two hundred were worn at one ball. Who made them, and of what, is not recorded.
  7. What was “The Brothers of Charity” of 1860, and was there ever a Sons of Malta lodge at Cassopolis?
  8. What do the Bedford lodge’s records hold? If the 1847 Pennsylvania lodge has a charter list or a building, it belongs beside Cassopolis.
## The pages
Read them yourself. Both books are free online through the University of Michigan, and the passage is short. The page photographs follow; the full books are linked under Sources.

stories.headline: The day 3,000 people came to watch one log
stories.short: The day 3,000 came to watch one log
stories.dek: Twenty-four men carried the first log of the Pioneer Log Cabin while a band played. Four weeks later the cabin was finished.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. At half past eight on the morning of 23 May 1923, a black walnut log twenty-six feet long was carried to its place by twenty-four men. A band played and the crowd sang. About three thousand people stood and watched, and many had driven up to fifty miles to be there.
It was the first log of the Cass County Pioneer Log Cabin. A note written on the back of one card of the day says fifty-two volunteers did the first morning’s work.

The logs came from families across the county, given from their own land. Each log was numbered, and a list kept the family’s name, the town and the kind of tree. The card printed for the occasion gives the whole job in one line: May 23 to June 20, 1923. Four weeks, from the first log to Pioneer Day.
The cabin still stands in Cassopolis today, as the Pioneer Log Cabin Museum.

stories.headline: Pick a date, and see what’s open
stories.short: Pick a date, and see what’s open
stories.dek: Tell the Visit & Plan page the day you’re coming. It shows the museums open that day, what’s on, and your own day on the map.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. Many of the valley’s museums are run by volunteers and open only a few days a week, some only in summer. Turning up to a locked door is the commonest way a day out goes wrong.
The Visit & Plan page now takes a date. Pick the day you’re coming and it shows which museums are open, using each place’s posted hours, and any festival on that day.
There are ready-made days out to start from, each one in an order that saves driving and opens in Google Maps with one tap. Or build your own day, and see it on the map with rough times.
Hours change, and the page can’t know about holidays, so check each place before you go.

stories.headline: Send someone an old postcard
stories.dek: Pick any card in the gallery, write on the back, and share it from your phone.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. A century ago this is how you told someone you were thinking of them: a picture of your town on the front, a few lines on the back, and a stamp.
Every card in the old postcard gallery now has a button under it: Send this postcard. Write who it’s to, your message and your name, and the back of the card is laid out as you type.
Then share it straight from your phone, or save the picture to post, text or print.
Nothing you write is sent to Project Scroll. The card is made on your own phone or computer.

stories.headline: Who told Shepard?
stories.dek: The only account of the 1846 lodge was written by a man who was a small child when it happened. Somebody told him. Who?
body: Cassopolis, Mich. Everything we know about the lodge of 1846 comes from one account, written by James M. Shepard and printed in Rogers’s History of Cass County in 1875.

Shepard did not see the lodge. He was a small child in 1846 and came to Cassopolis only in September 1868, as the village dentist. When he wrote, about 1875, three of the four charter men could still be found in or near the county: Dr. Evan J. Bonine at Niles, Jordan P. Osborn at Cassopolis, and Dr. Leander Osborn at Vandalia.
And he was not sure of everything he had been told. In the 1875 text the founders are “the charter (?) members,” with his own question mark. Mathews, reprinting the passage in 1882, dropped it.

So Case 1 asks: who told him? A founder, a member, a guest at the ball, the hotel’s keeper? The answer, if it survives, is in the record: in the books, the papers of the 1870s, or the lives of the men themselves.

Case 1 was first opened on 15 October with a different question, whether the lodge ever had a real charter. That question answered itself in Shepard’s own question mark, so the case now asks the one beneath it.

stories.headline: A depot, a water tower and three clues
stories.short: A depot, a water tower, three clues
stories.dek: An old real-photo postcard of a station somewhere in the valley. Can you name the town?
body: A small wooden depot. A water tower on iron legs. A field of tall grass, and not one person in sight. The card’s caption has been cut off, and the station sign blurred.
Clue one. The railroad here was the Michigan Central’s Air Line, which ran from Jackson to Niles.
Clue two. The town is in Cass County, east of Cassopolis.
Clue three. The Air Line came through in 1871, and the station was set up the same year.
stories.reveal: Vandalia. The caption at the foot of the card reads “R.R. Station Vandalia Mich.” The town’s other cards show the same depot with a train at the platform, and with passengers and a baggage cart. The Air Line between Jackson and Niles was abandoned in 1937.

stories.headline: The hotel that walked away
stories.dek: In 1867 the old hotel where the lodge held its ball was hauled across Cassopolis and turned into a mill. Where did it end up?
pic: /img/news/the-hotel-that-walked
The hotel’s block on the 1860 wall map of Cass County, Van Buren and Berrien counties
The hotel’s block on the 1860 Geil, Harley & Siverd wall map. Library of Congress.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. The old hotel stood at the northwest corner of Broadway and State Street, at the heart of the village.

It was the Union Hotel, where the lodge of 1846 held its grand ball. In 1852 the Masons held their first meeting under the same roof, and on the 1860 wall map of the county the engraver cut one word on its block: HOTEL.
Then, in 1867, the building was hauled across the village and turned into a mill, and a new hotel rose on its ground.
Where did the old hotel end up, and is any of it still standing? That is Case 2 on the board. The first sources are the county histories of 1882 and 1906, free to read online.

stories.headline: Fly over Cassopolis, laser point by laser point
stories.dek: 355,650 real laser points from the 2015 survey, in 3D, with the 1860 town plan laid on the ground.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. In 2015 an aircraft flew over Cass County firing laser pulses at the ground, hundreds of thousands a second, and timing each echo. Every dot in the new model is one of those echoes, from the blocks around the courthouse: 355,650 of them.
The buildings and trees stand where the laser found them, 125,189 points of roofs and 230,461 of trees, over the bare ground of the town.
Press “1860 plan” and the old town plan from the county wall map is laid on the ground beneath them. Raise the heights, tilt it, fly around it, or go full screen.
Fly over it, and you earn the Laser surveyor badge.

stories.headline: Stoves, lures, wagons and guitars
stories.dek: Twenty-three makers from the valley: what they made, how they ended, and where you can still see their work.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. For a century the towns of the valley made things the whole country knew by name.

Round Oak stoves came out of Dowagiac from 1871. James Heddon’s Sons made fishing lures there from 1902. Studebaker built wagons in South Bend, then cars. Gibson made mandolins and guitars in Kalamazoo, and C. G. Conn made band instruments in Elkhart.
The new Made in the Valley page follows twenty-three of them: who founded each one, what it made, when it peaked, how it ended, and the museums where its work is still on show.
Every maker is pinned on a map, and set on a timeline that runs from the 1850s to today.

stories.headline: Company D: the 85 men Dowagiac sent in 1861
stories.dek: Raised at Dowagiac in the summer of 1861: who they were, where they fought, and the nineteen who did not come home.
pic: /img/news/company-d-sixth-michigan
Monument Day, Dowagiac, Mich.: a great crowd around a monument, on a real-photo postcard
Monument Day, Dowagiac, on a real-photo postcard. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan.
body: Dowagiac, Mich. In the summer of 1861 a company was raised at Dowagiac, the second organized in Cass County, under Captain Charles E. Clarke. It became Company D of the Sixth Michigan Infantry.

The regiment gathered at Kalamazoo and left for the East on 30 August 1861, 944 strong. After garrison duty at Baltimore it went to New Orleans and the lower Mississippi, fought at Baton Rouge, and joined the assault on Port Hudson on 27 May 1863, where Lieutenant Frederick J. Clarke was killed. It ended the war as heavy artillery, and was discharged at Jackson, Michigan, on 5 September 1865.
Of its men, four were killed or died of wounds and fifteen died of disease. As in the whole war, sickness killed more of them than battle did.
The roll of all 85 men, as Mathews printed it in 1882, is now on the site, checked line by line against the page scans, with this week’s anniversaries from their service.
sources: Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), pp. 117–120, University of Michigan

stories.headline: Who was in town in 1860?
stories.dek: 331 names from the business directories printed beside the old town plans, with the men of Company D, in one roll you can search.
pic: /img/news/who-was-in-town-in-1860
The Cassopolis business directory beside the village plan on the 1860 wall map: hotels, merchants, physicians and surgeons
The Cassopolis directory beside the village plan, 1860 wall map. Library of Congress.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. Beside each town plan on the old county maps, the mapmakers printed a business directory: the lawyers, doctors, merchants, smiths, hotel keepers and county officers who paid to be listed.
Now 331 of those entries, from Cassopolis, Dowagiac, Niles and Paw Paw in 1860 and Goshen in 1861, are in one roll you can search by surname, trade or town, together with the 85 men of Company D.

A directory is not a census. It lists the people who paid to appear, so most farmers, labourers, women and children are not in it. But a directory line puts a person in a town, in a trade, in a year, and that is often the first step to finding a family.
Every entry links to its map, so you can find the name in the engraving yourself.

stories.headline: Eleven more old postcards
stories.dek: The Pioneer Log Cabin going up in 1923, the depots at Cassopolis and Vandalia, Chicago Street in Edwardsburg, Main Street in Niles and a steam shovel at White Pigeon.
pic: /img/news/eleven-more-old-postcards
Main Street, now Broadway, Cassopolis: a long arched brick block with awnings, on an early postcard
Main Street, now Broadway, Cassopolis, about 1905 to 1912. Private collection.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. Eleven more cards have joined the old postcard gallery, all from before 1931 and so in the public domain.

Two show the Pioneer Log Cabin going up in May and June of 1923. There are the Michigan Central depots at Cassopolis and Vandalia, the corner of State and Main in Vandalia, the north side of Chicago Street in Edwardsburg, a crowd on Main Street in Niles, and the long arched block on what was then Main Street, now Broadway, in Cassopolis.
White Pigeon joins the gallery for the first time, with a steam shovel at work on the paper mill track.
Every card can be searched, found on the map, and sent as a postcard of your own.

stories.headline: The harvest trail: a mill, an orchard and the stove town
stories.dek: Stamp three places in your passport this fall, from September to November, and earn the harvest badge.
pic: /img/news/the-harvest-trail
An orchard at its best, near Benton Harbor and St. Joseph, Mich., on a linen postcard
An orchard at its best, near Benton Harbor and St. Joseph, about 1930 to 1945. Boston Public Library, Tichnor Brothers Collection.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. Fall is harvest time in the valley, and the passport has a trail just for it.
The mill. Bonneyville Mill near Bristol, Indiana, a county park around a historic grist mill that still grinds flour, open Tuesday to Sunday until mid-November.
The orchard. Jollay Orchards near Coloma, where the same family has farmed since 1857: u-pick fruit, fresh cider and apple-cinnamon doughnuts.
The stove town. The Dowagiac Area History Museum, free, where the story of the Round Oak Stove Company is told.
Press “I’m here” at all three between September and November of the same year, and the harvest badge is yours. Check each place’s hours before you go.

stories.headline: A paper passport to stamp, and a teachers’ pack
stories.dek: A passport booklet with a stamp box for every place, a one-day field trip for classes, and the valley kitchen as a little book.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. The passport on Project Scroll lives in your phone: press “I’m here” at a museum, a walk stop, a table or a festival, and the stamp lands in it.
Now there is a paper one too. Print the booklet, fold it, and carry it. Every place in the valley has its own stamp box.
For teachers there is a one-day field trip, with the Broadway walk, the Local History Branch and the photo spots, and two worksheets: rephotographing an old postcard, and reading an old record.
And the recipes of the valley kitchen are now a little book to print and keep in the drawer.
